cheat_sheet.title: Dart and Flutter Foundations — Structural Cheat Sheet
cheat_sheet.introduction: This sheet turns Dart and Flutter Foundations into visible relationships. It is a reference for planning, tracing, debugging, and explaining—not a list to memorize.
cheat_sheet.why_it_matters: The level contributes directly to a Flutter mobile application. Each concept helps the learner move from an ambiguous task to a contract, a representation, a verified transition, and an explainable result.

mental_model.summary: Represent the work as widget trees, constraints, navigation graphs, and state transitions before translating it into implementation details.
reasoning_cycle: Model variables, state, constraints, and relationships

input_questions: What may be absent or malformed?
output_questions: What shape and state are promised?

core_concepts.title: Dart values, types, and null safety
core_concepts.rule: Types describe valid operations, while nullable and non-nullable references make absence an explicit part of the contract.

core_concepts.title: Variables, expressions, and functions
core_concepts.rule: Functions map typed parameters to results or documented effects, and local variables keep intermediate state bounded.

core_concepts.title: Conditions, loops, and exhaustive cases
core_concepts.rule: Control flow partitions states or repeats a transition; every branch and termination boundary must be accounted for.

core_concepts.title: Lists, maps, and immutable transformations
core_concepts.rule: Collections encode order or key lookup; creating transformed values makes state changes easier to trace.

core_concepts.title: Futures, async, and event timelines
core_concepts.rule: A Future represents one eventual result, and await orders dependent steps while the UI event loop remains responsive.

core_concepts.title: Widgets as immutable descriptions
core_concepts.rule: A widget is an immutable configuration that describes part of the interface; Flutter rebuilds descriptions when inputs change.

core_concepts.title: Stateful lifecycle and rebuilds
core_concepts.rule: State persists across rebuilds for the same element identity and must release subscriptions or controllers when disposed.

core_concepts.title: Packages, project structure, and debugging
core_concepts.rule: A Flutter project separates source, assets, dependencies, and tests; analyzer and inspector evidence guide debugging.

common_mistakes: Starting with syntax before defining the input-output contract.
Combining current state and a candidate update so rejection cannot be safe.
Treating an observed normal result as proof for every boundary.
Choosing a structure because it is familiar rather than because its operations match the constraints.
Ignoring empty, missing, duplicate, maximum-size, repeated, or out-of-order cases.
Hiding failures instead of representing loading, empty, rejected, and error states explicitly.
Optimizing before measuring the actual bottleneck or risk.
Explaining what the implementation does without explaining why its invariant proves correctness.
debugging_checklist: Can I restate the exact expected output?

Is the boundary inclusive or exclusive?
Can an invalid or repeated event mutate valid state?
Are asynchronous or external results stale, missing, or out of order?
Does the representation match the operation mix and constraints?
Did the repair pass the original failure and nearby regression cases?

lessons.title: Dart values, types, and null safety
lessons.goal: Model, apply, trace, and defend Dart values, types, and null safety within a cross-platform mobile experience.
lessons.learning_objective: Given a normal, boundary, or invalid case, the learner will use Dart values, types, and null safety to produce a valid result and explain the invariant or constraint that makes the result correct.

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: Dart values, types, and null safety is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. Types describe valid operations, while nullable and non-nullable references make absence an explicit part of the contract.

content_blocks.title: Formal structure
content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For Dart values, types, and null safety, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

content_blocks.title: See the system before the syntax
content_blocks.body: Use widget trees, constraints, navigation graphs, and state transitions. Draw the boundary, label inputs and outputs, then trace one transition at a time.

inputs: The data or event that activates Dart values, types, and null safety
outputs: A value, decision, or visible state matching the contract
A preserved or deliberately updated next state
Evidence explaining acceptance or rejection

constraints: Inputs must match the declared shape and permitted boundary.
A rejected input must not corrupt the previous valid state.
The output must be representable by the current application workflow.
Every external or user-provided value is validated before use.
invariants: The governing relationship remains true: Types describe valid operations, while nullable and non-nullable references make absence an explicit part of the contract.
At most one documented commit occurs for one accepted transition.
Invalid input leaves the last valid state unchanged.
step_by_step_reasoning: Restate the problem as a testable input-output contract.
List state variables and separate current state from a candidate update.
Write constraints as predicates with visible boundary choices.
Apply the structural rule for Dart values, types, and null safety.
Trace the normal case one transition at a time.
Trace an exact boundary and one invalid case.
Compare observed output and preserved invariants with the contract.
Record the first divergent state if the check fails.

worked_examples.scenario: An input violates one required relationship or arrives in an unsupported state.

Keep the previous valid state unchanged.
Return a specific, non-sensitive explanation or recovery path.

common_mistakes: Beginning implementation before defining the required output.
Changing state before the input or transition has been validated.
Memorizing the label 'Dart values, types, and null safety' without applying its governing relationship.
Testing only one convenient normal case and assuming boundaries behave identically.
edge_cases: The smallest valid input or empty valid structure, when allowed.
The largest documented input, count, depth, size, or duration.
A duplicate, repeated event, retry, or already-completed transition.
Malformed, missing, stale, unauthorized, or otherwise out-of-contract input.
debugging_strategy: Freeze the first input that produces a wrong observable result.
Write the expected trace beside the observed trace.
Locate the first row where state, constraint, or output diverges.
Repair the rule or boundary responsible for that first divergence.
Rerun the failing case plus one normal, one boundary, and one rejection case.

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: Variables, expressions, and functions is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. Functions map typed parameters to results or documented effects, and local variables keep intermediate state bounded.

content_blocks.title: Formal structure
content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For Variables, expressions, and functions, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: Packages, project structure, and debugging is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. A Flutter project separates source, assets, dependencies, and tests; analyzer and inspector evidence guide debugging.

Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

project.title: Dart and Flutter Foundations: Flutter Mobile Application
project.real_world_context: A small team needs a cross-platform mobile experience that remains understandable under normal, boundary, invalid, and recovery conditions. The learner is responsible for the reasoning model and verifiable outcome.
project.problem_definition: Create a level-appropriate Flutter mobile application that demonstrates all eight skills from Dart and Flutter Foundations. The artifact must show how inputs become outputs, how state changes, which constraints are enforced, and how failures recover.
project.project_brief: Begin with diagrams, tables, and contracts. Build the smallest complete version, test it against the supplied case categories, record the first divergent state, repair it, and submit both the artifact and reasoning evidence.

outputs: primary task result
visible loading/empty/error or rejected state
test evidence
decision record

governing_rules: Types describe valid operations, while nullable and non-nullable references make absence an explicit part of the contract.
Functions map typed parameters to results or documented effects, and local variables keep intermediate state bounded.
Control flow partitions states or repeats a transition; every branch and termination boundary must be accounted for.
Collections encode order or key lookup; creating transformed values makes state changes easier to trace.
A Future represents one eventual result, and await orders dependent steps while the UI event loop remains responsive.
A widget is an immutable configuration that describes part of the interface; Flutter rebuilds descriptions when inputs change.
State persists across rebuilds for the same element identity and must release subscriptions or controllers when disposed.
A Flutter project separates source, assets, dependencies, and tests; analyzer and inspector evidence guide debugging.

constraints: Use only the languages, components, or structural interactions supported by the target application environment.
Do not hide invalid input, unavailable data, or failure behind a successful-looking state.

Record assumptions and unsupported cases explicitly.
The submitted result must be reproducible from the included instructions.

optional_extensions: Add a second representation and compare which relationships become easier to inspect.

lessons.title: Navigation routes as a graph
lessons.goal: Model, apply, trace, and defend Navigation routes as a graph within a cross-platform mobile experience.
lessons.learning_objective: Given a normal, boundary, or invalid case, the learner will use Navigation routes as a graph to produce a valid result and explain the invariant or constraint that makes the result correct.

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: Navigation routes as a graph is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. Screens are nodes and allowed transitions are directed edges carrying typed arguments and returning optional results.

content_blocks.title: Formal structure
content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For Navigation routes as a graph, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

content_blocks.body: Use widget trees, constraints, navigation graphs, and state transitions. Draw the boundary, label inputs and outputs, then trace one transition at a time.

outputs: A value, decision, or visible state matching the contract

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: Gestures, hit targets, and feedback is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. Gesture handling maps pointer sequences to semantic actions and must provide discoverable, immediate state feedback.

content_blocks.title: Formal structure
content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For Gestures, hit targets, and feedback, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

content_blocks.title: See the system before the syntax
content_blocks.body: Use widget trees, constraints, navigation graphs, and state transitions. Draw the boundary, label inputs and outputs, then trace one transition at a time.

inputs: The data or event that activates Gestures, hit targets, and feedback

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: Accessible widget semantics is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. Labels, roles, values, focus order, scalable text, and sufficient targets preserve meaning across assistive input modes.

content_blocks.title: Formal structure
content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For Accessible widget semantics, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

project.title: Widgets, Layouts, Navigation and Forms: Flutter Mobile Application
project.real_world_context: A small team needs a cross-platform mobile experience that remains understandable under normal, boundary, invalid, and recovery conditions. The learner is responsible for the reasoning model and verifiable outcome.
project.problem_definition: Create a level-appropriate Flutter mobile application that demonstrates all eight skills from Widgets, Layouts, Navigation and Forms. The artifact must show how inputs become outputs, how state changes, which constraints are enforced, and how failures recover.
project.project_brief: Begin with diagrams, tables, and contracts. Build the smallest complete version, test it against the supplied case categories, record the first divergent state, repair it, and submit both the artifact and reasoning evidence.

outputs: primary task result
visible loading/empty/error or rejected state

decision record

governing_rules: Parents pass constraints down, children choose a permitted size, and parents position the resulting boxes.
Flex layouts divide finite main-axis space by fixed needs and flex factors while cross-axis alignment controls placement.
A scrolling viewport needs bounded constraints and should lazily build large sequences to control memory and work.
Screens are nodes and allowed transitions are directed edges carrying typed arguments and returning optional results.
A form collects named values, applies local and cross-field constraints, and submits only a valid snapshot.
Themes encode shared design tokens, while responsive composition selects structures that satisfy current width and content constraints.
Gesture handling maps pointer sequences to semantic actions and must provide discoverable, immediate state feedback.
Labels, roles, values, focus order, scalable text, and sufficient targets preserve meaning across assistive input modes.

starter_materials.scaffold_policy: Level 2 leaves validation and recovery sections for the learner.

mandatory_features: Demonstrate Flutter's constraints layout rule and cite its governing rule in the decision record.
Demonstrate Row, Column, Flex, and available space and cite its governing rule in the decision record.
Demonstrate Scrolling lists and bounded viewports and cite its governing rule in the decision record.
Demonstrate Navigation routes as a graph and cite its governing rule in the decision record.
Demonstrate Forms, controllers, and validation and cite its governing rule in the decision record.
Demonstrate Themes and responsive composition and cite its governing rule in the decision record.
Demonstrate Gestures, hit targets, and feedback and cite its governing rule in the decision record.
Demonstrate Accessible widget semantics and cite its governing rule in the decision record.
constraints: Use only the languages, components, or structural interactions supported by the target application environment.
Do not hide invalid input, unavailable data, or failure behind a successful-looking state.
Keep current valid state recoverable until a candidate transition passes validation.
Do not embed secrets, real credentials, personal data, or private endpoints.
Make all important output and error states accessible and testable.
Record assumptions and unsupported cases explicitly.
The submitted result must be reproducible from the included instructions.

test_cases.expected: one correct output and valid next state

test_cases.condition: second valid input with different data

test_cases.expected: accepted only if contract includes it

test_cases.condition: valid retry after a controlled failure

debugging_checklist: Freeze a reproducible failing input.
Compare expected and observed traces.
Find the first divergent state.
Check the constraint at that transition.
Repair cause before symptoms.
Rerun the failure and adjacent cases.
Confirm state recovery and accessible feedback.
Record the limitation if the case remains unsupported.
completion_checklist: All eight level skills appear in the artifact or evidence.
The input-output contract is complete.
The structural model matches the implementation or decision flow.
All eight required test categories have evidence.
The rubric self-score totals 100 possible points.
No secret, real credential, or sensitive personal data is included.
Submission instructions reproduce the result.
Reflection names one failure, repair, and justified improvement.
submission_requirements: README with setup or review instructions

rubric.evidence: inputs, outputs, constraints, diagram, and milestones
mandatory behavior matches the project contract
clear responsibilities, transitions, and dependency boundaries
normal, boundary, invalid, repeated, and failure cases
usable states, safe handling, and recovery feedback
setup, decisions, limitations, evidence, and reproducible instructions
first divergence, repair, trade-off, and next iteration

common_failure_conditions: The result handles only one normal case.
State changes before validation.
A level skill is named but not demonstrated.
The diagram disagrees with the implemented flow.
A failed dependency leaves a false success state.
Submission evidence cannot be reproduced.
reflection_questions: Which assumption changed after the first trace?
Where did expected and observed state first diverge?
Which invariant prevented the most serious failure?
What trade-off did you make among clarity, cost, performance, accessibility, safety, or flexibility?
What evidence would you collect before a wider release?
optional_extensions: Add a second representation and compare which relationships become easier to inspect.
Add property-based or generated boundary cases without duplicating existing tests.
Measure one performance, quality, or risk indicator and justify an improvement threshold.
Design a migration or compatibility plan for one changed requirement.
project.acceptable_outcome_example: A submission may use the supplied contract and state templates, implement one complete primary journey, show all required failure states, and provide eight passing test records plus one documented limitation. The exact implementation remains the learner's work.

prompts.prompt: Restate the final input-output contract in one sentence.
Describe the first state where expected and observed behavior diverged.
Explain the repair and the invariant or constraint it restored.

cheat_sheet.title: State Management and Application Architecture — Structural Cheat Sheet
cheat_sheet.introduction: This sheet turns State Management and Application Architecture into visible relationships. It is a reference for planning, tracing, debugging, and explaining—not a list to memorize.
cheat_sheet.why_it_matters: The level contributes directly to a Flutter mobile application. Each concept helps the learner move from an ambiguous task to a contract, a representation, a verified transition, and an explainable result.

mental_model.summary: Represent the work as widget trees, constraints, navigation graphs, and state transitions before translating it into implementation details.
reasoning_cycle: Model variables, state, constraints, and relationships

input_questions: What may be absent or malformed?
output_questions: What shape and state are promised?

core_concepts.title: Local, shared, and derived state
core_concepts.rule: Place mutable state at the narrowest owner that serves all consumers and compute derived values instead of storing duplicates.

core_concepts.title: Explicit state transitions
core_concepts.rule: Represent each user or system event as an action that transforms a known previous state into one next state.

core_concepts.title: Notifiers and observable dependencies
core_concepts.rule: Observers rebuild only when the values they depend on change; clear subscription ownership prevents leaks and stale views.

core_concepts.title: Unidirectional data flow
core_concepts.rule: State flows down to views and events flow back to an owner, creating a cycle with one authoritative source of truth.

core_concepts.title: Repositories and service boundaries
core_concepts.rule: A repository exposes domain-focused data operations while hiding whether data came from network, database, or cache.

core_concepts.title: Dependency injection and test seams
core_concepts.rule: Dependencies enter through constructors or providers so production implementations can be replaced by controlled test doubles.

core_concepts.title: Loading, data, empty, and error states
core_concepts.rule: Asynchronous screens need an explicit finite state model so no result or failure becomes an accidental null case.

core_concepts.title: Layered feature architecture
core_concepts.rule: Presentation, domain, and data layers point through narrow contracts, limiting the effect of change and simplifying tests.

common_mistakes: Starting with syntax before defining the input-output contract.
Combining current state and a candidate update so rejection cannot be safe.
Treating an observed normal result as proof for every boundary.
Choosing a structure because it is familiar rather than because its operations match the constraints.
Ignoring empty, missing, duplicate, maximum-size, repeated, or out-of-order cases.
Hiding failures instead of representing loading, empty, rejected, and error states explicitly.
Optimizing before measuring the actual bottleneck or risk.
Explaining what the implementation does without explaining why its invariant proves correctness.

lessons.title: Local, shared, and derived state
lessons.goal: Model, apply, trace, and defend Local, shared, and derived state within a cross-platform mobile experience.
lessons.learning_objective: Given a normal, boundary, or invalid case, the learner will use Local, shared, and derived state to produce a valid result and explain the invariant or constraint that makes the result correct.

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: Local, shared, and derived state is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. Place mutable state at the narrowest owner that serves all consumers and compute derived values instead of storing duplicates.

content_blocks.title: Formal structure
content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For Local, shared, and derived state, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: Unidirectional data flow is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. content_blocks.title: Formal structure
content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For Unidirectional data flow, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: Dependency injection and test seams is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. Dependencies enter through constructors or providers so production implementations can be replaced by controlled test doubles.

content_blocks.title: Formal structure
content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For Dependency injection and test seams, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

content_blocks.body: Use widget trees, constraints, navigation graphs, and state transitions. Draw the boundary, label inputs and outputs, then trace one transition at a time.

project.title: State Management and Application Architecture: Flutter Mobile Application
project.real_world_context: A small team needs a cross-platform mobile experience that remains understandable under normal, boundary, invalid, and recovery conditions. The learner is responsible for the reasoning model and verifiable outcome.
project.problem_definition: Create a level-appropriate Flutter mobile application that demonstrates all eight skills from State Management and Application Architecture. The artifact must show how inputs become outputs, how state changes, which constraints are enforced, and how failures recover.
project.project_brief: Begin with diagrams, tables, and contracts. Build the smallest complete version, test it against the supplied case categories, record the first divergent state, repair it, and submit both the artifact and reasoning evidence.

outputs: primary task result
visible loading/empty/error or rejected state
test evidence
decision record

governing_rules: Place mutable state at the narrowest owner that serves all consumers and compute derived values instead of storing duplicates.
Represent each user or system event as an action that transforms a known previous state into one next state.
Observers rebuild only when the values they depend on change; clear subscription ownership prevents leaks and stale views.
State flows down to views and events flow back to an owner, creating a cycle with one authoritative source of truth.
A repository exposes domain-focused data operations while hiding whether data came from network, database, or cache.
Dependencies enter through constructors or providers so production implementations can be replaced by controlled test doubles.
Asynchronous screens need an explicit finite state model so no result or failure becomes an accidental null case.
Presentation, domain, and data layers point through narrow contracts, limiting the effect of change and simplifying tests.

starter_materials.scaffold_policy: Level 3 leaves architecture and core transitions partially open.

mandatory_features: Demonstrate Local, shared, and derived state and cite its governing rule in the decision record.
Demonstrate Explicit state transitions and cite its governing rule in the decision record.
Demonstrate Notifiers and observable dependencies and cite its governing rule in the decision record.
Demonstrate Unidirectional data flow and cite its governing rule in the decision record.
Demonstrate Repositories and service boundaries and cite its governing rule in the decision record.
Demonstrate Dependency injection and test seams and cite its governing rule in the decision record.
Demonstrate Loading, data, empty, and error states and cite its governing rule in the decision record.
Demonstrate Layered feature architecture and cite its governing rule in the decision record.
constraints: Use only the languages, components, or structural interactions supported by the target application environment.
Do not hide invalid input, unavailable data, or failure behind a successful-looking state.
Keep current valid state recoverable until a candidate transition passes validation.
Do not embed secrets, real credentials, personal data, or private endpoints.
Make all important output and error states accessible and testable.
Record assumptions and unsupported cases explicitly.
The submitted result must be reproducible from the included instructions.

test_cases.expected: one correct output and valid next state

test_cases.condition: second valid input with different data

test_cases.expected: accepted only if contract includes it

test_cases.condition: valid retry after a controlled failure

maximum documented size
duplicate or retry
out-of-order or stale result
malformed or unauthorized input
debugging_checklist: Freeze a reproducible failing input.
Compare expected and observed traces.
Find the first divergent state.
Check the constraint at that transition.
Repair cause before symptoms.
Rerun the failure and adjacent cases.
Confirm state recovery and accessible feedback.
Record the limitation if the case remains unsupported.
completion_checklist: All eight level skills appear in the artifact or evidence.
The input-output contract is complete.
The structural model matches the implementation or decision flow.
All eight required test categories have evidence.
The rubric self-score totals 100 possible points.
No secret, real credential, or sensitive personal data is included.
Submission instructions reproduce the result.
Reflection names one failure, repair, and justified improvement.
submission_requirements: README with setup or review instructions

rubric.evidence: inputs, outputs, constraints, diagram, and milestones
mandatory behavior matches the project contract
clear responsibilities, transitions, and dependency boundaries
normal, boundary, invalid, repeated, and failure cases
usable states, safe handling, and recovery feedback
setup, decisions, limitations, evidence, and reproducible instructions
first divergence, repair, trade-off, and next iteration

common_failure_conditions: The result handles only one normal case.
State changes before validation.
A level skill is named but not demonstrated.
The diagram disagrees with the implemented flow.
A failed dependency leaves a false success state.
Submission evidence cannot be reproduced.
reflection_questions: Which assumption changed after the first trace?
Where did expected and observed state first diverge?
Which invariant prevented the most serious failure?
What trade-off did you make among clarity, cost, performance, accessibility, safety, or flexibility?
What evidence would you collect before a wider release?
optional_extensions: Add a second representation and compare which relationships become easier to inspect.
Add property-based or generated boundary cases without duplicating existing tests.
Measure one performance, quality, or risk indicator and justify an improvement threshold.
Design a migration or compatibility plan for one changed requirement.
project.acceptable_outcome_example: A submission may use the supplied contract and state templates, implement one complete primary journey, show all required failure states, and provide eight passing test records plus one documented limitation. The exact implementation remains the learner's work.

Describe the first state where expected and observed behavior diverged.
Explain the repair and the invariant or constraint it restored.

What is the safest and most valuable next improvement?

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: HTTP clients and typed serialization is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. Transport responses become trusted domain values only after status checks, decoding, and field validation.

content_blocks.title: Formal structure
content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For HTTP clients and typed serialization, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: Cache-aside and freshness decisions is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. Read from a cache under an explicit freshness policy, refresh from the source, and define behavior when either side fails.

content_blocks.title: Formal structure
content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For Cache-aside and freshness decisions, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: Resilient offline-first data flow is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. An offline-first feature exposes local state immediately, synchronizes in the background, and communicates pending or conflicted changes.

content_blocks.title: Formal structure
content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For Resilient offline-first data flow, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

content_blocks.title: See the system before the syntax
content_blocks.body: Use widget trees, constraints, navigation graphs, and state transitions. Draw the boundary, label inputs and outputs, then trace one transition at a time.

project.title: APIs, Local Storage and Offline Applications: Flutter Mobile Application
project.real_world_context: A small team needs a cross-platform mobile experience that remains understandable under normal, boundary, invalid, and recovery conditions. The learner is responsible for the reasoning model and verifiable outcome.
project.problem_definition: Create a level-appropriate Flutter mobile application that demonstrates all eight skills from APIs, Local Storage and Offline Applications. The artifact must show how inputs become outputs, how state changes, which constraints are enforced, and how failures recover.
project.project_brief: Begin with diagrams, tables, and contracts. Build the smallest complete version, test it against the supplied case categories, record the first divergent state, repair it, and submit both the artifact and reasoning evidence.

outputs: primary task result
visible loading/empty/error or rejected state
test evidence
decision record

governing_rules: Transport responses become trusted domain values only after status checks, decoding, and field validation.
Asynchronous work needs lifetime rules so obsolete responses cannot overwrite newer screen state.
Use key-value storage for small preferences, not relational data or secrets that require stronger protection.
Local tables preserve structured offline state; versioned migrations keep existing installations readable after schema change.
Read from a cache under an explicit freshness policy, refresh from the source, and define behavior when either side fails.
Queued mutations need stable identities, retry policies, and a deterministic rule for resolving concurrent edits.
Tokens require protected storage, limited lifetime, redaction, and a clear logout or revocation path.
An offline-first feature exposes local state immediately, synchronizes in the background, and communicates pending or conflicted changes.

common_mistakes: Starting with syntax before defining the input-output contract.
Combining current state and a candidate update so rejection cannot be safe.
Treating an observed normal result as proof for every boundary.
Choosing a structure because it is familiar rather than because its operations match the constraints.
Ignoring empty, missing, duplicate, maximum-size, repeated, or out-of-order cases.
Hiding failures instead of representing loading, empty, rejected, and error states explicitly.
Optimizing before measuring the actual bottleneck or risk.
Explaining what the implementation does without explaining why its invariant proves correctness.

Which state is allowed to change?

Is the boundary inclusive or exclusive?
Can an invalid or repeated event mutate valid state?
Are asynchronous or external results stale, missing, or out of order?
Does the representation match the operation mix and constraints?
Did the repair pass the original failure and nearby regression cases?

lessons.title: Unit, widget, and integration tests
lessons.goal: Model, apply, trace, and defend Unit, widget, and integration tests within a cross-platform mobile experience.
lessons.learning_objective: Given a normal, boundary, or invalid case, the learner will use Unit, widget, and integration tests to produce a valid result and explain the invariant or constraint that makes the result correct.

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: Unit, widget, and integration tests is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. Choose the smallest test boundary that proves the behavior: pure logic, rendered interaction, or multi-screen integration.

content_blocks.title: Formal structure
content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For Unit, widget, and integration tests, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

content_blocks.body: Use widget trees, constraints, navigation graphs, and state transitions. Draw the boundary, label inputs and outputs, then trace one transition at a time.

lessons.learning_objective: Given a normal, boundary, or invalid case, the learner will use Analytics, privacy, and failure monitoring to produce a valid result and explain the invariant or constraint that makes the result correct.

content_blocks.title: Start with the relationship
content_blocks.body: Analytics, privacy, and failure monitoring is easier when you stop treating it as a tool to memorize. Begin with what enters the problem, what must leave it, and what is allowed to change. Collect only purposeful events, gain appropriate consent, avoid sensitive fields, and connect failures to actionable context.

content_blocks.title: Formal structure
content_blocks.body: Represent the task as a transition F(input, current_state) -> (output, next_state). For Analytics, privacy, and failure monitoring, F is valid only when its preconditions hold, its output matches the declared shape, and every stated invariant remains true. Validation occurs before an irreversible commit.

project.title: Testing, Performance, Accessibility and Release: Flutter Mobile Application
project.real_world_context: A small team needs a cross-platform mobile experience that remains understandable under normal, boundary, invalid, and recovery conditions. The learner is responsible for the reasoning model and verifiable outcome.
project.problem_definition: Create a level-appropriate Flutter mobile application that demonstrates all eight skills from Testing, Performance, Accessibility and Release. The artifact must show how inputs become outputs, how state changes, which constraints are enforced, and how failures recover.
project.project_brief: Begin with diagrams, tables, and contracts. Build the smallest complete version, test it against the supplied case categories, record the first divergent state, repair it, and submit both the artifact and reasoning evidence.

outputs: primary task result
visible loading/empty/error or rejected state
test evidence
decision record

governing_rules: Choose the smallest test boundary that proves the behavior: pure logic, rendered interaction, or multi-screen integration.
Profile frame timing and rebuild scope before changing code; stable inputs and smaller observers reduce unnecessary work.
Large assets, caches, controllers, and subscriptions consume bounded resources that need sizing and disposal policies.
Verify semantics, focus, text scale, contrast, orientation, and error recovery across complete user journeys.
Translate messages and format dates, numbers, direction, and plural forms according to locale rather than concatenating fragments.
Request the minimum permission at the moment of need and align declared capabilities, privacy notices, and behavior.
Collect only purposeful events, gain appropriate consent, avoid sensitive fields, and connect failures to actionable context.
Automated checks produce signed builds, while staged rollout, monitoring, and rollback control release risk.

starter_materials.scaffold_policy: Level 5 supplies only constraints, acceptance criteria, and review checkpoints.

mandatory_features: Demonstrate Unit, widget, and integration tests and cite its governing rule in the decision record.
Demonstrate Rebuild measurement and render performance and cite its governing rule in the decision record.
Demonstrate Memory, images, and resource lifetime and cite its governing rule in the decision record.
Demonstrate Accessibility audits and inclusive flows and cite its governing rule in the decision record.
Demonstrate Internationalization and locale-sensitive data and cite its governing rule in the decision record.
Demonstrate Platform permissions and store readiness and cite its governing rule in the decision record.
Demonstrate Analytics, privacy, and failure monitoring and cite its governing rule in the decision record.
Demonstrate Continuous delivery and staged release and cite its governing rule in the decision record.
constraints: Use only the languages, components, or structural interactions supported by the target application environment.
Do not hide invalid input, unavailable data, or failure behind a successful-looking state.
Keep current valid state recoverable until a candidate transition passes validation.
Do not embed secrets, real credentials, personal data, or private endpoints.
Make all important output and error states accessible and testable.
Record assumptions and unsupported cases explicitly.
The submitted result must be reproducible from the included instructions.

test_cases.expected: one correct output and valid next state

test_cases.condition: second valid input with different data

test_cases.expected: accepted only if contract includes it

test_cases.condition: valid retry after a controlled failure

edge_cases: empty or minimum
maximum documented size
duplicate or retry
out-of-order or stale result
malformed or unauthorized input
debugging_checklist: Freeze a reproducible failing input.
Compare expected and observed traces.
Find the first divergent state.
Check the constraint at that transition.
Repair cause before symptoms.
Rerun the failure and adjacent cases.
Confirm state recovery and accessible feedback.
Record the limitation if the case remains unsupported.
completion_checklist: All eight level skills appear in the artifact or evidence.
The input-output contract is complete.
The structural model matches the implementation or decision flow.
All eight required test categories have evidence.
The rubric self-score totals 100 possible points.
No secret, real credential, or sensitive personal data is included.
Submission instructions reproduce the result.
Reflection names one failure, repair, and justified improvement.
submission_requirements: README with setup or review instructions

rubric.evidence: inputs, outputs, constraints, diagram, and milestones
mandatory behavior matches the project contract
clear responsibilities, transitions, and dependency boundaries
normal, boundary, invalid, repeated, and failure cases
usable states, safe handling, and recovery feedback
setup, decisions, limitations, evidence, and reproducible instructions
first divergence, repair, trade-off, and next iteration

common_failure_conditions: The result handles only one normal case.
State changes before validation.
A level skill is named but not demonstrated.
The diagram disagrees with the implemented flow.
A failed dependency leaves a false success state.
Submission evidence cannot be reproduced.
reflection_questions: Which assumption changed after the first trace?
Where did expected and observed state first diverge?
Which invariant prevented the most serious failure?
What trade-off did you make among clarity, cost, performance, accessibility, safety, or flexibility?
What evidence would you collect before a wider release?
optional_extensions: Add a second representation and compare which relationships become easier to inspect.
Add property-based or generated boundary cases without duplicating existing tests.
Measure one performance, quality, or risk indicator and justify an improvement threshold.
Design a migration or compatibility plan for one changed requirement.
project.acceptable_outcome_example: A submission may use the supplied contract and state templates, implement one complete primary journey, show all required failure states, and provide eight passing test records plus one documented limitation. The exact implementation remains the learner's work.

prompts.prompt: Restate the final input-output contract in one sentence.
Describe the first state where expected and observed behavior diverged.
Explain the repair and the invariant or constraint it restored.
Name one design trade-off and the evidence behind your choice.
What is the safest and most valuable next improvement?

optional_mastery_challenge.title: Optional Mastery Transfer
optional_mastery_challenge.prompt: Transfer the level's eight governing rules to a new version of a cross-platform mobile experience with one changed constraint, one new failure state, and one stricter evidence requirement.
required_outputs: change-impact table across all eight skills
normal, boundary, invalid, and recovery traces
success_criteria: The changed constraint is applied consistently.
No unaffected invariant is silently removed.
The new failure state has visible recovery behavior.
Evidence distinguishes old and new behavior.
